response:
Retrieval-augmented generation systems depend on a stable semantic manifold: the embedding space must remain consistent enough that a query vector and a document vector encoded at different times still occupy geometrically meaningful relative positions. The central question here is what happens to that manifold when you fine-tune only the query encoder (or only the document encoder) on new data while leaving the other side frozen, then periodically re-index a subset of documents rather than recomputing the entire corpus — a pattern that is extremely common in production because full re-indexing is expensive. The expert worry that beginners miss entirely is anisotropy collapse under asymmetric drift: fine-tuning one encoder causes its output distribution to shift toward a lower-dimensional subspace (a well-documented anisotropy phenomenon in transformer-based encoders), but because the other encoder hasn't moved, the two sides now live in geometrically misaligned subspaces — dot products between them lose discriminative power not because individual embeddings are wrong, but because the geometry of the joint space has degenerated. Compounding this, iterative partial re-indexing creates a temporally heterogeneous index where old document embeddings (from the pre-fine-tuning encoder) and new ones coexist, meaning a single query vector must simultaneously retrieve across two different manifolds with no explicit signal about which regime any given document belongs to. The retrieval degradation is therefore not monotonic or easily detected by standard recall metrics on a held-out test set — it appears as subtle, query-distribution-dependent ranking failures that only surface under distribution shift in the query stream.

When the query encoder collapses toward a low-dimensional subspace, all query vectors begin occupying a narrow cone in the embedding space — a phenomenon measured concretely by Ethayarajh (2019) who showed that upper layers of BERT-family models can have effective dimensionalities as low as 20–50 out of 768, with anisotropy quantified by the average cosine similarity between random vector pairs approaching 0.9+ in degenerate cases. The dot-product failure mode is score compression with false uniformity: because query vectors are now nearly collinear, their dot products with the fixed document embeddings cluster in a tight numerical range, destroying the score spread that ranking depends on — the top-ranked document still receives the highest score, but the margin between rank-1 and rank-100 collapses to near-zero, making the ranking extremely sensitive to numerical noise. This is precisely why MRR@10 and Recall@100 evade it: both metrics are rank-ordinal, they only ask whether the relevant document appears in the top-k, not whether the score margins are meaningful — so if the correct document was retrievable before drift, it may still appear at rank 3 even in the degraded space, just with a score gap of 0.003 instead of 0.3. The insidious downstream consequence is that score-thresholded filtering and fusion break silently: production RAG pipelines commonly gate retrieval on a minimum similarity threshold (e.g., cosine ≥ 0.75) or blend dense and sparse scores via linear interpolation (as in REALM and RAG-Token), and when score distributions compress, either everything passes the threshold (flooding the LLM context with noise) or nothing does (inducing retrieval collapse). Facebook's RAG paper (Lewis et al., 2020) and subsequent BEIR benchmark work (Thakur et al., 2021) both surface retrieval failures under domain shift, but neither instruments score-margin statistics — the community's standard eval harness is blind to this failure by construction. Partial re-indexing makes it worse because the score range of new documents (encoded by the drifted encoder) differs systematically from old documents, introducing a recency bias artifact where newer index entries win not on semantic relevance but on score-scale compatibility with the drifted query encoder.
